div.head: Remarks.
Ingomar.
div.p: The story upon which this play (a translation from the German), is founded, is interesting and affecting. It exhibits filial duty in its most beautiful form, and treats of the mys terious passion of Love (exquisite delusion! captivating error!) with delicacy and feeling. It is simple and natural, and extremely well told.

Myron is a poor armourer, dwelling in a humble cottage in the city of Massilia. He–
'in the fields
Labours and toils all day;
Then must he hammer at the forge by night;
And when the tillage rests, that cannot he,
But sets out heavily laden, as now, with arms,
To offer them for sale in neighbouring villages." His wife Actea shares, if not his toils, at least his anxieties. "1,' she pleads
'remain at home,
'Tis true–yet go I forth in thought, and carry
With him the burden of the goods: with him I pant
Up the rough mountain's slippery path, and feel
The pelting storms that soak his weary limbs.' They have an only daughter, Parthenia, a beautiful young Greek girl, whom, in parental parlance, they are anxious to see 'settled.' Parthenia has been often wooed, but never won. Medon became her suitor :
'Oh! he was old,
Gray–headed, gouty, coarse." Evander proposed, but with no better success:
'He had a fox's cunning,
With a hyæna's heart and monkey's form.'

Now comes their rich neighbour, Polydor, a mongrel and a monkey–grub. Him, too, she despises. Her angry mother thinks that Miss may be expecting the 'Man in the Moon' to 'pop the question.' For what can she be waiting? The daughter's reply is a recitation of the mother's well–learnt lesson upon love, which the oblivious old lady seems, conveniently, to have forgotten !

Polydor (calculating curmudgeon !) brings his prudence to bear upon his concupiscence. His hopeful offspring (according to his own account) are–
Gluttonous pigs, wild, rude, unruly boys." Shall he, 'at great expense,' hire a Domine to school them? No.–Gentleness is the best teacher, and the pretty Parthenia is gentle. Commerce frequently calls him to the market– place. Is it safe to leave his well–filled coffers to the questionable guardianship of a mercenary slave? Then he
grows old, and is often sick. Who so proper to pour out his physic, and make ready his warm room for him, as a true wife? Parthenia shall be pedagogue, cash–keeper, and nurse ! Polydor pleads his passion like a man of business. But what, inquires Parthenia, will he do for the poor armourer? His answer is so sordid and unsatisfactory that his 'pretty rosebud dismisses him in no very complimentary terms.
'Did I hear right?........the armourer's child
Scorns me, the rich descendant of the gods.' He vows vengeance against Myron:
'I'll take No more swords of him, I'll buy up the rights
Of all his creditors, summon him to justice–
I will–I'll drive him from his house and home–
Ay, from the city–him and his saucy child.
That will I!–Yes, I'll force out his last drachma.'

The environs of Massilia are infested by a band of robbers called the Alemanni, who descend from the adjacent moun– tains and carry off men and cattle with impunity. Suddenly the sad news arrives that Myron has been kidnapped by these free–booters, and that thirty ounces of bright silver are de– manded for his ransom. Adrastus, Amyntas, Neocles, (all friends 1) are pathetically, but in vain, appealed to by Parthenia. Polydor, who stands aside, could hug. these gold worshippers! As a last resource, the heart–broken daughter. turns to that chuckling malignant:
'Forget, forgive, –restore my father to me,
I'll be thy wife, will bind myself thy slave.'
He makes a mock of her misery.
A brave and noble thought passes over her despair. She will to the mountains!–Alone and in darkness? The gods will protect and guide her!

In that lofty and romantic region, the Cevennes, the haunt of the Alemanni, Alastor, one of the band, announces to his comrades, that though he and his foraging party have made prize of neither cattle nor coin, yet they have brought a 'fan.– ciful pretty thing of a girl,' who–delivered herself voluntarily into their hands, for the purpose of being introduced to their chief to offer ransom for a slave. A general growl greets this unprofitable booty, which only subsides when Parthenia is led forth. The mutual recognition of father and child move not the sluggish sympathy of these marauders. The chief (Ingomar) asks what sort of a ransom she has to offer. Her reply is characteristic and beautiful:
'Jewels of more value
Than all the gold of earth: a faithful wife's
Prayers, to her last breath–a daughter's tears–
A rescued household's deathless gratitude–
The blessing of the gods, whose liberal hands
Recompense deeds of mercy, thousand–fold.' 'Is that the ransom?" demands one of the Alemanni. 'Has she deceived us?' furiously cries another. The chief commands silence. Parthenia proceeds:
'My mother and myself Will labour with him: we will live on crusts, And all the surplus of our daily toil Be yours, till the full ransom be accomplished."

'But where's our surety? Hast brought it with thee?" inquires Ingomar. Parthenia's own person shall be the surety. 'Burden us with a woman!' shouts the impetuous cattle–stealer. Parthenia will be no burden, but a help :
'These willing hands
Shall do more work than twenty pining slaves ;–
I spin,
Can weave your garments, and prepare your meals,
Am skilled in music and can tell brave tales,
And sing sweet songs to lull you to repose.

The strange bargain is struck, and Myron, in an agony of surprise and distraction, is hurried off the scene. Parthenia keeps her word. Instead of openly repining. her tears are seldom seen; and, when seen, are soon wiped away. She wreathes the drinking–cups of her wild associates with garlands of fair flowers, and holds playful discourse with Ingomar. He listens intently to her sweet voice, and gazes with rapture at her lovely face and form. But when she touches upon one all–absorbing subject–love, and describes that high and holy passion with tenderness and truth,–when she sings plaintively the song that asks and answers the question 'what love is?' he sucks in the delicious poison until his brain fires with delirium. ––But, the paroxysm past, he sinks into moody abstraction, repeating to himself the last lines of that syren–song–
'Two souls with but a single thought,
Two hearts that beat as one."

The nature of Ingomar is changed. The fierceness of his spirit is subdued. He is become listless and languid; an irresolute and feverish dreamer. This inaction suits not his ferocious band. Their passion is war and plunder. They murmur. 'Why not choose another chief?" vociferates one. 'Do away with the cause of this metamorphosis,' retorts another. `=Remove from the camp this Greek girl, to hear whose idle tales and love–songs the once warlike Ingomar lolls lazily on the green sward, the live–long day! They hit upon a project that will not only rid them of this perplexing enchantress, but put money in their purses:–Sell her for a slave to the merchants from Carthage, whose ship appears in sight on the distant waters. The ship is hailed, a boat reaches the shore, Parthenia is seized and all but dragged on board, when her frantic cries bring Ingomar to her rescue. The robbers hold angry parley with their chief, and threaten resistance to his will. The dormant and still proud spirit of Ingomar is fired. He bids them choose their own path–he is weary of holding such a turbulent troop in check. As for the Greek girl, she shall be his, and a fifth part of the spoil (his share) he will give them for her ransom. His terms are accepted, and the Alemanni go their way.

Safe and free! In the first transports of delight and
. gratitude Parthenia kisses the hard sunburned hand of Ingomar, and bursting into a flood of tears, bids him farewell! She would seek her loved home, and be restored to her parents, who, in suspence and sorrow, wait her too lingering return. True to his word, Ingomar will not detain his captive. Yet he forewarns her of the perils that beset her path. He bids her–
*Think of the dark wood, the dizzy cliff,
The dreadful chasms, and the roaring floods,
The wolf and bear.'

He resolves to be her escort. An involuntary thrill of distrust and fear blanches her cheek, and makes her heart trembie! But 'tis only a transient emotion. The frank and noble nature of Ingomar fully assures her that she can have no more honourable guide than himself, and she trusts to his protection.

Arrived at the tall cliff that looks down upon Massilia, the travellers make a pause. The hour of parting is come. Ingomar must retrace his slow and solitary steps through the bleak wilderness, to his mountain–home; Parthenia, light– hearted and swift–footed, will trip to her father's cottage within the city that stands in view. Painful is the interval! The hearts of both are deeply moved! But why attempt to describe what every kindred spirit will at once anticipate? They must not, cannot part! Ingomar will turn Greek, and Parthenia will become his bride !

Myron, somewhat reluctantly, consents to receive Ingomar into his house; but he must discard his rough bear–skin mantle, and relieve his head and chin of their superabundant bristles. He must deliver up his trusty sword, too, turn a peaceable man, and work alternately in the field and in the smithy. All this will Ingomar cheerfully do for Parthenia!

An alarm spreads through the city. A numerous host of the dreaded Alemanni descend from the hills. The gates are closed. The guards are doubled. Suspicion falls upon Ingomar, and Myron is summoned to appear before the council. 'I said he was a spy! a traitor !' shrieks the terrified Actea. And who is her authority for this false charge? The malignant Polydor. In vain Ingomar asserts his innocence–the Alemanni but pass Massilia en route to pay off an old grudge the Allobrogi. The Timarch, or chief functionary, now appears upon the scene. His Grace offers Ingomar a liberal bribe if he will betray his countrymen to the Greeks. But this, Ingomar will never do–not even to obtain Parthenia. In the sequel, his sacrifice to honour is amply rewarded. Polydor is publicly disgraced and driven out of the city, the Alemanni are welcomed as Massilia's future brothers and allies, and Marthenia becomes his bride.

To Mrs. Lovell (the wife of an author who has done the drama good service), the stage is indebted for this elegant and spirited version of Ingomar. Mr. Anderson (during his brief season), produced it at Drury Lane, where it was received with applause. The excellent acting of Miss Van– denhoff in Parthenia contributed greatly to its success.

div.head: Scene I.
div.stage: Massilia, the Market–place, in front of an Archway which crosses the back of the Stage. In the foreground, on the right, Myron's and another house, spinning–wheel and basket in front of Myron's house – Opposite to it the house of Polydor.
Enter Actea, from the House, R.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: The sun is nearly set–the city gates
Will quickly close, yet Myron comes not home:
Parthenia, too–wild girl! freed from her task,
Flies like a bird unfettered from her cage.
Parthenia! daughter! child !

div.stage: Enter Parthenia, R. U. E.

sp.l: Well, mother dear !

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Ah! truant, see, here lies thy work undone,
And evening near.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I've spun enough to–day;
And yonder are our neighbours gathering olives–
I'll help them.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: No! thou shalt remain with me;
And listen, wild one:–thou hast long enough
Wasted the hours in trifling children's play,–
'Tis time to end it;–so now sit thee down,
And, if thou canst, be serious for once.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Yes, mother dear–I hear.

div.stage: She seats herself listlessly at the wheel.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Bethink thee, child,
This Polydor is rich–a man in years,
'Tis true, but rich–a widower, indeed,
But much respected, and of quality:
He asks thy hand–dost listen?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Yes, oh yes.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Ah, so thou always say'st; yet I may speak,
Talk by the hour, while all thy busy thougnts
Wander thro' fields and woods, as thou thyself,
Chasing the butterflies; but now 'tis time,
Though with spring blood, to think of coming autumn,–
'Tis time to think of marriage ;–yet already
Thou hast rejected Medon.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh! he was old,
Gray–headed, gouty, coarse–

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Evander, then.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Evander! – Yes, he had a fox's cunning,
With a hyæna's heart and monkey's form.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Mad foolish girl! go, trample down thy fortune,
Until repentance comes too late! Thou think'st
Thyself unequalled, doubtless; lovely, rich.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Young am I, mother; joyous, happy, too.
And you, you love me! what can I wish more?
Yes–you do love me!

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Love thee–ah! and well
Dost thou deserve our love!
Why do I fold thee thus within my arms?
We love thee, but thou lovest us not.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Not love thee, mother?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: No! or as our will
So would thine own be–thou wouldst let us choose
Thy husband.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No, dear mother, no–not him.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: What dost thou hope for, then? Perhaps thou think'st
The man in the moon would be thy fitting spouse:
What waitest thou for, I say?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Why do I wait?–
I'll tell thee, mother.–I was but a child,
And yet I marked it well: you sang to me
Of Hero and Leander, and their love;
And when I asked thee, wond'ring, what love was,
Then, with uplifted hands and laughing eyes,
Thou told'st me how, into the lonely heart,
Love sudden comes unsought, then grows and grows,
Feeble at first, like dawn before the sun,
Till, bursting every bond, it breaks at last
Upon the startled soul with hope and joy,
While every bounding pulse cries, 'that is he
Who carries in his breast my heart, my soul :
With him, oh, may I live, and with him, die!'
So, when old Medon and Evander came
To woo, I laid my hand upon my heart,
And listened, listened, but no ! all was still,
All silent; no response, no voice;–and so
I'm waiting, mother, till my heart shall speak!

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Good gods! 'tis thus we let our old tongues prattle
While young ears listen. [Aloud.] So, thou foolish child,
'Tis that thou waitest for–thy heart must speak!
I prattled nonsense, a child's tale, a dream !
I tell thee, there's no second will come to thee
Like Polydor, so rich, so honourable.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Honourable!
Beats down my needy father in his wares,
Higgles, and bargains.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: That thou understandest not.
He is a careful and a saving merchant:–
Think, think, my child–say yes–for my sake, do,
Say yes, my child.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Hold, mother.–I will wander never more
Through woods and fields; like other girls, will spin,
Will work, will read thy wishes in thine eyes;
But him, that Polydor, I cannot, will not–
No, never–never!

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Never?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Thou art angry !

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Away! have I not cause enough for anger
Thy parents now grow old, and long for rest;
Thy father, a poor armourer, in the fields
Labours and toils all day;
Then must he hammer at the forge by night;
And when the tillage rests, that cannot he,
But sets out, heavily laden, as now, with arms,
To offer them for sale in neighbouring villages.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Poor father!

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Poor? poor, indeed! Then I remain at home
'Tis true,–yet go I forth in thought, and carry
With him the burden of the goods; with him. I pant
Up the rough mountain's slippery path, and feel
The pelting storms which soak his weary limbs,
And think, that even now, in the dark valley,
The wild Allobrogi.or fierce Alemanni
Attack him, rob him, murder him, perhaps!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh, mother, mother !

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: So must I weep, and weep. But thou–
Thou whom he loves, for whom he e'en would die–
For whom he risks his blood, his limbs, his life–
Thou, thou mightst spare him from all weariness,
Mightst dry my tears, make happy our old age,
Be so thyself. But no! thou canst, yet wilt not.
Go, go, thou selfish and ungrateful child.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ungrateful! no, ye gods, that am I not!
Ungrateful to my father!–No! and yet
For me does the rough storm beat on his head;
For me he staggers 'neath his heavy loads,
And totters panting up the mountain sides.
Yes, yes, I'll show my mother she is wrong;
It shall not be. But yet, what would I do?
Unite myself to age, to avarice?
That is to die! to die–'twere better far!
But yet it must be so–farewell, sweet dreams!
And once the future lay so bright before me:
There shone the scarce–formed hope, the mystic joy–
Let all be fancy–love be but a dream;–
All is a fable that adorns our life,
And but the passing day alone is real!
Well, be it so.–Parthenia wakes to duty!
And now, sweet visions of my youth, farewell.
My father now shall labour hard no more–
Shall rest. Ah! who comes here? 'tis Polydor!
I'll fly–yet no! I will remain: if my happiness
Must be put up for sale, then let the price
Be well secured for which I barter it.
What looks he? pride, ill–temper, avarice–
And I his wife! It makes my heart grow cold.
sp.stage: [She approaches her spinning–wheel, at which she sits to work.

div.stage: Enter Polydor, L.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: This will not do, the slave impoverishes me;
There is no doing without a wife–it must be.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Does he not look as tho' he had the weight
Of the world upon his thoughts? and yet, I wager,
He only thinks on pigs and geese.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Nothing replaces Kallinike to me:
She was a true heart–she could work, could save!
But then the armourer's daughter–could she?
Ah, she is there herself! she's young, she's pretty,
So,–yes–no–well, so be it.–
Good day, fair maid. Good day!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Say, rather, evening, when the sun is sinking.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Can it be evening while thy bright eyes shine?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Away, sir, with fine words–we will speak plainly:
They tell me you propose to marry me.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Ah! that is plain–that's coming to the point;
Aha! her fond impatience cannot wait.
Yes, yes, such is my thought.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: My mother told me so, ––and yet I wonder
Thy choice should fall on me: how soon, it seems,
You have forgotten Killinike!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Forgotten? No, indeed: a man like me
Forgets not gold, nor goods, nor the worth of goods;
And that was she to me;–yet weighty reasons
Press on me a new choice, –my children–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ay, poor orphans!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Poor they are not: they are troublesome,
Gluttonous pigs, wild, rude, unruly boys.
Shall I, at great expense, hire a schoolmaster
From Samos or Miletus? Gentleness
Best rules rough strength, and thou indeed art gentle.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Gentle! oh yes, as gentle as a lamb
Led to the sacrifice.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Besides, I am often far from home–my business
Now calls me to the market, now to the harbour;
And shall a slave meanwhile keep house for me,
And farm, and warehouse? guard my well–filled coffers?
That only can a wife, only a true wife.
And then, too, I grow old, am often sick;
And who would tend me then? make ready for me
The warm room, and prepare my drink and physic?
Ah! only a fond wife.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh, my poor heart!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: 'Tis thou shalt be that wife, and thou shalt make me
Strong, young again; thy love, my pretty rosebud–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Away–and listen now to me:
Thou know'st my father tills the fields by day,
And at the anvil works by night, and then
Upon his shoulders carries to a distance
His wares for sale; that he is now in years,
And wants repose:–say then, when I am thine–
Say, wilt thou think of my poor father?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Ay, certainly I will,–how could I otherwise?
Yes, yes, I will,–I will think of thy father.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: And do; –what wilt thou do for him?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Oh, he shall be advanced, for he will be
My father–in–law, the father–in–law of Polydor,
Of the rich Polydor; and from the gods
My lineage springs:
Think what an honour! from the gods, my child.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: But honour gives not food; –what wilt thou do?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Well, in the first place, buy, as hitherto,
His wares at a good price.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: At a good price!–That is, good for thyself.
Well, and what more?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: What more! Why, then again, then will I–
Observe me now, and bear in mind, girl–know
I will take thee without dowry–yes, entirely
Without a dowry; true as thou'rt alive,
I'll take thee–ay, without a drachma!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: But what do for my father?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Is not that
To do? and plenty, too, I think.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No more?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: No more! almost too much.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: By all the gods, yes, –it is quite too much;
And so, good evening.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: No, stay–thou shalt not go without an answer.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: An answer thou shalt have, and mark it well.–
Procure your children, sir, a schoolmaster
At any price, and whence you please; a slave
To guard your house, attend to bolts and bars;
Shouldst thou fall sick, there, at the corner yonder
Go, bid the huckster sell thee wholesome herbs;
Mix for thyself thy medicine and thy drink.
But know, for me there grows no bitterer herb
On earth than sight of thee! Now, mark it well–
This is my answer,–thou poor heartless miser.
So fare thee well, descendant of the gods!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.stage: [Standing looking after her for a time.]
sp.l: What's that? did I hear right? she turns me out!
Me, the rich Polydor! The armourer's child
Scorns me, the rich descendant of the gods,
As though I were her father's fellow workman;
Disdains me! mocks me!–There's no bitterer herb
On earth than sight of me! Yes, and it shall
Be bitter to thee, and to others too.
I'll have revenge! – What shall I do? I'll take
No more swords of him, I'll buy up the rights
Of all his creditors, summon him to justice;
I will; –I'll drive him from his house and home,
Ay, from the city–him and his saucy child.
That will I!–Yes; I'll force out his last drachma.
Oh, I'll not rest until I've had revenge !
sp.stage: While violently agitated, he walks up and down.

div.stage: Enter Lykon, L.

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: The road straight on, he said. Ay, here's the market;
Near here must be the house, I'll take my chance.
sp.stage: [He goes to the next house to Myron's, and knocks.
sp.l: Hillo! come forth, open–I bring bad news:
Shut as you will your ears, misfortune knocks
So loud that you must hear it in the end.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Ah! what does the man want

sp.speaker: Theano.
sp.l: Who calls so loud?

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: Come out, and you will hear.

div.stage: Enter Theano, from the doorway, R.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What do you want, man? speak!

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: You are Myron's wife.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: The armourer's? I? no–my husband's dead !

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: Then thank the gods–better death than slavery.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Ah! who? what? Myron, dost thou say?

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: Is taken prisoner, seized by the Alemanni.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Taken prisoner! seized! Ah! that's good news, indeed.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Myron a prisoner?

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: Yes; I beheld it with these eyes.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Ye gods! Myron!
sp.stage: Enter Neocles, Elphenor, Amyntas, and Citizens, through archway.
sp.l: Here come his friends.

sp.speaker: Neo.
sp.l: Ah! what alarm is this?

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Elphenor, Adrastus, here! This man brings news;
Myron is prisoner–seized by the Alemanni.

sp.speaker: Neo.
sp.l: How! speakest thou true?

sp.speaker: Elp.
sp.l: How did it happen? tell me.

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: It was beside the coast; I was preparing
Within the woods a yard to fit my boat,
When came a man along, heavily laden:
I stood concealed by a thick bush, and saw him
Lay himself down to rest upon the moss,
When suddenly from out the thicket rings,
Like a wolf's howl, the shout of the Alemanni.

div.stage: Enter Actea, coming down the steps from her house, without observing those present.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: There! she has carelessly left the spinning–wheel.
Ah! what is this?

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: With that they rushed upon him,
Seized on his goods, and, with rough acts and words,
Demanded who he was; and when he said
He was an armourer of Massilia,
They shouted with delight, 'he must with them;'
And with loud cries they drove him, bound, along.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: An armourer! bound! and driven along? Ah, tell me
Who was the armourer? Speak! who was the man?

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.stage: [After a pause; to the others, with his eyes cast down.]
sp.l: Say, is that Myron's wife?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Myron's! ye gods.
Then Myron was it? speak! why stand ye dumb?
No, no, it was not Myron! tell me – quick!

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: He is taken by the Alemanni.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Woe is me!

sp.speaker: Neo.
sp.l: She swoons!

sp.speaker: Elp.
sp.l: She falls to the ground!

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Help!–help! carry her in ;–
I will console her.

sp.speaker: Amy.
sp.l: Are these barbarians from the mountains?

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: Yes:
The Alemanni, who, some three weeks since,
As well you know, regardless of the treaty,
Broke from their native fastness in the mountains,
Destroyed the land, seized upon travellers,
And drove the cattle from the fields: and these
Are they who now have taken wretched Myron.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Where is the man who brings this fearful news?
Art thou he? speak! my father–is it true?
Sawest it thyself?

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: Scarcely ten paces from me
Were the old man and the exulting robbers.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: And thou escap'dst while he–

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.l: Within the thicket
I stood alone, and ventured not to stir
Until the band moved off; and then I fled ;
But the old man, perceiving me, called after–
'Hear me! I am Myron of Massilia,
The armourer :–for the sake of all the gods,
Go, tell them there, that they may ransom me.'
Then one of the wild men called, 'If they will,
They must pay thirty ounces of bright silver:
That is his price.' Amidst their shouts I fled,
And they with haste bore him towards the Cevennes.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: And he a prisoner!–No–back, foolish tears!
Clear be mine eyes, and thou, my soul, be steel!
They carried him, thou say'st, to the Cevennes.
And they demand a ransom! House and fields
Are mortgaged–what is to be done? Yet friends
Remain.–
Adrastus, you will help us? You,
Amyntas, – you grew up with him; think how
You shared with him the games of childhood,
The cares of age: you'll rescue him–you can.
Oh! speak, kind friends; say yes–lend us the ransom.

sp.speaker: Amy.
sp.l: I? thirty ounces? would I had so much
For my own children.

sp.speaker: Neo.
sp.l: The sea carries all
My wealth, and who may count on wind and waves?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Ah ha!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Take pity, that the gods may pity you;
That thy ship may return in safety back,
The yoke of bondage and the weight of poverty
Never oppress thy children,–rescue him.
Oh, let my mother's grief, my tears, prevail!

sp.speaker: Neo.
sp.l: I cannot help you.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Amyntas,–you.

sp.speaker: Amy.
sp.l: I cannot.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh, friendship, what a fable! my poor father!

sp.speaker: Herald.
sp.l: Room, citizens, for the Timarch!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ah! the Timarch?
He is saved!
Massilia will protect her children!

div.stage: Enter Herald, with a white wand, preceding the Timarch, L.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: Room, I say, for the Timarch.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.stage: [Sinking at the feet of the Timarch.]
sp.l: Rescue! help!

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Speak, maiden! wherefore dost thou ask our help?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Save him! Myron the armourer–my father–
In the mountains–the Alemanni drag him thither;
Oh! rescue him from slavery.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: A citizen
In danger!–What wouldst thou have us do?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Let the trumpets sound–the citizens seize their swords;
And let Massilia's power demand her son!
Rescue their captive prey from the wild robbers,
And give him, free again, to his free home.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: That cannot be. for, by an ancient law,
Made in the time Massilia, then scarce founded,
Was struggling for its unsecured existence,
In battle with the inhabitants of the coast,
It was decreed, the care of individuals
Should never compromise the entire state,
But that each man must look to his own safety.
Massilia but protects her citizens
So far as reach the shadows of her walls;
And that has Myron overstepped; nor can we,
To favour him–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: To favour! [Springing up.] No–not favour–
'Tis right! Is not Massilia firmly now
Established? reaches not her powerful arm
Far, far beyond the shadow of her walls?
Her free born son is wronged, and the state with him,–
He is imprisoned; –Timarch, set him free!

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: I cannot: were a single stone displaced
In the fabric of justice, the whole house would fall
At once :–see to it yourself, I cannot help you.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Have pity.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: With the gods alone dwells pity;
On earth dwells justice; and for private right
I cannot do a public wrong.––Make way!

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: Room, room, I say, for the Timarch!

div.stage: [Exeunt Timarch, preceded by Herald, &c.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Pity–mercy!
Alas, no ear listens to my complaint;
All leave me, all forsake me! O, ye gods!
sp.stage: [She conceals her face in both hands, kneeling.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I cannot help you.'
Oh! I could hug you, you gold worshippers,
For what you said. 'I cannot help you–no.'
Right! all are gone–all! And now comes my turn,一
She shall remember it.–Ah ha!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I will, I must find help; I will to Polydor,
Will sacrifice myself to save my father.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Well, Polydor is not far off: what wouldst thou?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Here in the dust behold me at thy feet.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Ah! see now, in the dust and at my feet!
Art ill, that thou dost seek so rank a weed?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Forget, forgive, restore my father to me,
I'll be thy wife, will bind myself thy slave.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Indeed!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Will faithfully take care of house, of home,
And goods, for thee; will comfort thine old age,
And watch over thy children.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: See, now see!
And wilt thou do all this? all–really all?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: All this, and more; pay but this ransom for him,
Restore my father.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Ah! and thirty ounces,
I think you ask? No, no, that is too much :
I am a man who follow good advice,
So will I yours : –hire tutors for my children.
Protect my house with bolts and bars, and then,
If I am ill, will buy me medicine,
There at the corner, from the huckster,–so
I think you said. The advice was good, and now
I'll give you mine:–rescue thy father
Thyself; go, seek him yonder in the mountains;
Plead with thy flippant eloquence to move
The barbarians there, and try if any one
Of them will value it at thirty ounces,
And pay thy father's ransom. Ha! ha! ha!
Thou hast spurned Polydor, see if they'll outbid him :–
And so, good bye, my thorny rose, good bye!
Now I'm revenged. Aha!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: What thought is this that over–comes despair,
And fills my swelling heart with inspiration?
Oh! fool, that only came to goad my sorrow;
It is the gods command thee thus to speak!
Away, away! the night comes quickly on.
Parthenia, up! thy labour now begins–
Away! Ah, my poor mother,–Theano, Theano!
My mother? speak.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: She has wept herself to sleep.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: The gods be thanked!–Theano, I bequeath
My mother to thy care: I go to the mountains.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Now? it grows dark.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: All here is clear and bright. Farewell!

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What mean'st thou? not alone?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: The gods
Are with me; –so, farewell.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Parthenia, hear me.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Away, away!

div.head: Scene I.–
div.stage: In the Cevennes.—A Wood, densely arched with trees—where the bushes are less thick is seen a mass of wild rack. In the background, L., a half–extinguished fire, several Alemanni, clothed in skins, sleeping in a circle round it; near it, shields, helmets, spears, cups, and pitchers, scattered about—in the background, some tents of skin.
In the foreground, R., lie Ambivar, Novio, and Trinobantes, about a mass of rock, throwing dice.—Ingomar is seen asleep under a tree, against the trunk of which lean his sword and shield.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: One throw more, the stake is mine.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: Down—that's what I call luck.

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: Now it is my turn.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: What is it worth?

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: I have at home a black colt, two years old,
Fleet as the winds; will that do?

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Done! I stake two fat rams against him.

div.stage: [While they are gambling—
Enter Alemanni, L., driving on Myron, with a load of wood on his shoulder.

sp.speaker: Alem.
sp.p: Now, slave, throw down the wood, and hew it for our evening fire; here's the axe,—be quick.

div.stage: [Exit, L.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: It all seems like a dream: O, wretched Myron !
Miserable that you are! I—I the slave
Of these barbarians! I, but yesterday
Massilia's citizen, a happy husband,
Fond father, and free man—and now to–day—

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: Drink, slave, drink!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: 'Tis done; the colt is mine.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: Ten!

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: Thunder and lightning !

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Alas! Not all my goods would be enough
To ransom me from slavery !—And I am old:
If I were young, I would take courage then,
And try to escape. Oh! is there no hope for me!

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.p: Slave, didst hear? mead, mead! I'll tear thy deaf ears from thy skull; mead, slave, mead !

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Here is mead!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Now, again. What is it Trinobantes?

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: My armlet here.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: My belt against it;—do you say done?

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: Done!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Will they not pay
My ransom? Oh! ye gods, mock not my trust,
But bring me home again!
And let me die in my dear daughter's arms!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: After them! quick, quick ! Slay them !
So—why! I have been dreaming!—I was wounded—
The battle was decided—the day was ours!
Then, how they fled! what booty we obtained !
How many prisoners !—and yet it was a dream !
Well—I'll to sleep again.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: Lost! Now I've had enough for to-day.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Once more!

sp.speaker: Samo.
sp.l: 'Tis dinner-time.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Well, come on—'twas mine.

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: No! mine, I say !

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Thou liest!

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: Dog, dost thou play false?

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Dog! dogs bite.

div.stage: [He is about to strike Novio down, but the blow is arrested by the latter, and they struggle for the axe.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: What now?

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: Murderous villain!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Leave hold.

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: Who dares?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I! Dare you dispute me? your leader?
Peace, I command you !

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: Away!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: His blood or thine!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Back, back—I say.
But one step more, I'll send you to the shades.
Now go at once;—
Climb, Novio, yonder rock,—look for Alastor.
Take thine axe, and hew us wood,—begone!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Good—the time will come!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: You, Ambivar, prepare our supper; Samo,
Bring in the cattle. Away, all of you.

div.stage: [They go off at different sides.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Defiance to me—their chief—son of their chief?
Lightnings of heaven! To Myron. Ah, slave, come here
Bring drink.
sp.stage: [Myron hands him a goblet, from which he drinks.
sp.l: How it refreshes me!
Now, slave, kill time for me.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: I?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: What is your name?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Mine? Myron, sir!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Mine–Myron, sir?
Ha! ha! so chirps the linnet's brood in the nest!
And then he looks as sour as though he had swallow'd
A sloe-bush! Speak—who art thou?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Alas! alas!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: By all the gods, what dost thou whine for thus,
Thou silly fool? What ails thee? Thou hast here
Both food and drink in plenty; and at night
Thou restest on soft moss. Once at our home,
We'll make a smithy for thee;—there thou shalt work
And hammer as before, and live as merrily—

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: And callest thou the loss of liberty nothing?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: What liberty? Poor fool, you make me laugh!
Liberty! and dost thou miss liberty?
That thou didst not possess, man, when we took thee:
Old age already held thee in its yoke;
Youth only is strong, and strength alone is free.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: My freedom's lost!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Fool! what knowest thou of freedom?
With us is freedom. — She lives in the open air;
In woods she dwells; upon the rocks she breathes;
Now here, now there;—not caring for to-day—
No, nor providing for to-morrow!
Freedom is hunting, feeding, fighting, danger:
That, that is freedom,—that it is which makes
The veins to swell, the breast to heave and glow.
Ay, that is freedom,—that is pleasure–life!
But you, in your dark walls, a den, a prison,
You have life only to be sad.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: I was born in them, sir;—
’Tis there dwell harmony, law, and order;
There a true wife, there a dear daughter;—all
The best things I possess on earth are there.
Oh, my poor wife! my daughter!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Old fool! What? tears again, tears about women!
Why, thou art thyself a woman. What are they?
Vain, foolish playthings, only born to bear
And serve; to eat and drink;
To squat among the cattle, feed the children;
To oil their hair, and look at themselves in brooks.
Women! Were I a god,
And had the world to make, I'd make no women!
And thou crying for women!— out of my sight,
Old baby!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Sir, thou art angry;—yet wert thou,
Like me, a wretched slave—

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I? I a slave. — When Ingomar shall fall,
Unconquered will he mount among the gods!

div.stage: [A horn is heard.]

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Hush! silence! yonder is Alastor's horn:
They're here.

div.stage: Myron retires up stage.
Enter Novio, L.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Is it they? Speak!

sp.speaker: Novio.
sp.l: Yes.—Yonder come they through the valley:
Alastor, hastening before the rest,
Climbs nimbly up the cliff.—Look, he is here!

div.stage: Enter Alastor hastily, from back of stage. Alemanni enter from different parts, and gather around him.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: How now, Alastor, what hast brought? what news:
What booty?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: None,—I come with empty hands.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Dost thou speak true? The citizens of Avenna
Send every year their fat herds to the pasture
Upon the mountains. Met you none of these?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: No—not a single hoof.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Bad news, indeed.
So thou bringest?––

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: Nothing!
Yet stay—one thing I've brought,
A fanciful pretty thing of a girl.

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: What! a woman? Aha, that's good!
What do we want with women?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: A girl?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: She gave herself up to us. We lay in wait
In the thicket yonder, watching for the cattle,
When steps rustled in the distance, voices were heard,
And she came hastily bounding along,
Heedless of the stony path or burning sun.
Then rushed we out; the boy who was her guide
Fled; but she stood there still, and keeping off
Our out–stretched weapons with her naked hand,
Cried, 'Hold—I seek ye,—are ye Alemanni?'

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ah, a brave girl!

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: And you?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: We laughed. —Thou seekest us, said we;
Now thou hast found us, thou art become our booty;
But she, freeing herself angrily from our grasp,
Cried, 'No, no, not your booty—I am come
To treat for ransom for your slave, and so
Give me safe escort to your chief.'

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: A ransom for your slave!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: If so, she speaks the truth—she has free escort.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: So, at that word, we liberated her,
To guide her on her way to Ingomar.
She followed us with rapid steps, and if
We turned, she drew herself up thus, and waved
Her hand like this. Ha! ha! You would have thought
She was the chief, and we but her attendants.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: Ah! she has a heart in her body!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: For what slave's ransom comes she?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: For Myron's of Massilia.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: For him! The crying baby—the old woman!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Freed, ransomed, and by her!
Oh, tell me,—say, has she not glossy hair,
Her eyes bright, and her limbs like the young fawn's,
Her voice sweet as the nightingale's? so sweet!
Oh say, sir, is it not my child?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: See for yourself, she is here!

div.stage: Enter Parthenia, L. U. E., surrounded by several Alemanni.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Parthenia, my child! my dear dear child!
’Tis thou! thine eyes beam on me. — Oh, ye gods,
Let me not go mad!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: My dear father!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: There, there he cries again! Ye gods of thunder,
The fellow's like a rain cloud!

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: A truce to tears and whimpering.—Woman,
Thou seekest Ingomar—this is he.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: They say thou'rt come to treat for this man's ransom.
What is thy offer?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Jewels of more value
Than all the gold of earth: a faithful wife’s
Prayers, to her latest breath—a daughter's tears—
A rescued household's deathless gratitude—
The blessing of the gods whose liberal hands
Recompense deeds of mercy, thousand–fold.
Look—kneeling at your feet, a fainting child
Implores a gray–haired father's liberty.
He is infirm, old, valueless to you;
But, oh, how precious to his widowed home!
Give him, then, up—oh, give him to me.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Give him!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Is that the ransom?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: For nothing!—Has she deceived us?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Silence!
Woman, thy father is booty to our tribe:
Were he but mine, I'd give him to thee freely,
If only to be rid of his tears and sighs.
But if thou hast deceived us, and dost dare—

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Enough—
There need no threats.—I but misunderstood you,
Thinking you had human hearts—I'll mend of that,
And speak now to your interests.—
You ask gold for his ransom—he has none;
But he has strength and skill that yet may earn it,
With opportunity afforded him.
Here there is none –he cannot pay a drachma.
Keep him; and slavery, gnawing his free heart,
In a few weeks shall leave you but his bones.
But set him free, my mother and myself
Will labour with him: we will live on crusts,
And all the surplus of our daily toil
Be yours, till the full ransom be accomplished.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: That's not without some sense; but where is our surety
The compact should be kept?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: It shall not fail
For lack of that—I'll leave with you a pledge
Dearer to him than liberty or life.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Hast brought it with thee?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ay.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Show it.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Myself.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Child—thou art mad!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thyself.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: If you but knew
How precious to him is his child, you'd not
Despise the hostage.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: No—this shall not be!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: We did not ask your counsel;
It's a strange fancy, and yet—psha! no, no,
Burthen us with a woman!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No–no burthen;–
I'll be a help to you; these willing hands
Shall do more work than twenty pining slaves ;–
You do not guess my usefulness: I spin,
Can weave your garments, and prepare your meals,
Am skilled in music, and can tell brave tales,
And sing sweet songs to lull you to repose.
I am strong, too, –healthy both in mind and body;
And, when my heart's at ease, my natural temper
Is always joyous, happy, gay–Oh, fear not!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Troth! there's some use in that;–thy father can only cry.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Say yes–say yes, and set him free!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: No, she is mad

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Silence! Comrades, what think you? speak!
sp.stage: [He retires with Trinobantes. – Myron and Parthenia are left alone in the front.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Unhappy girl, what wouldst thou do?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: My father,
Thou shall be free.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Would not our friends, –the Timarch–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: All, all were deaf; and so alone I came
To break thy chains.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Oh, that I had never lived
To hear these words! Better to see thee fall
In the bear's den than here to be with these
Whom nature but made human out of scorn.
And thou, my child ! Taking her to his bosom. No, no!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Father, it must be so: my mother grieves–
Oh, dry her tears.
I am yet young and strong;
I could bear easily what would kill thee–
Father, be free, and let me stay !

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Here, where death threatens thee? ay, worse than death,
Violence, insult!–Never! sooner this dagger––

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Give it to me, and fear not. I will live
Worthy of thee or die !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I will it so–the girl shall stay.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: Let us keep both.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: No, that would be dishonest: she has come
Trusting, and shall not be deceived.
Woman, your wish is granted:––we take thee
As hostage for the other, and he is free.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Be thank'd, ye gods!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: No, no! I am your slave,
And will remain–let her return.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Who cares what you desire? Away with thee!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: My child–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Go, go, my father.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: Quick–away, away!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No, seize him not so roughly–see, he goes–
Willingly goes–away–delay no longer–
Go. go.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Villains, I will return, for the destruction of you all!

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Strike him dead!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh, save him !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: No, send him forth in safety–
'Tis my command.

sp.speaker: Tec.
sp.l: Away with him!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Parthenia, my child–farewell!
sp.stage: [Exit, L., dragged off by the Alemanni

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Farewell!
He is gone, and I shall never see him more!
sp.stage: [She clasps her hands before her face, and stands sobbing in the foreground.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.stage: [Who has been standing on a rock looking at the proceedings of his Followers.]
sp.l: No violence! Ho! how he runs! and now
He stops and cries again! Poor fearful fool!
It must be strange to fear :–now, by my troth,
I should like to feel, for once, what 'tis to fear!
But the girl–Leaning forward. Ha! do I see right? you weep!
Is that the happy temper that you boast?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh, I shall never see him more

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: What! have we,
For a silly old man, got now a foolish
And timid weeping girl? I have had enough
Of tears.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Enough, indeed, since you but mock them!
I will not–no, I'll weep no more.
sp.stage: [She quickly dries her eyes, and retires to the background.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: That's good; –come, that looks well;
She is a brave girl! she rules herself, and if
She keep her word, we have made a good exchange.–
'I'll weep no more.'–Aha! I like the girl.
And if––Ho! whither goest thou?
sp.stage: [To Parthenia, who is going off with two goblets.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Where should I go? to yonder brook, to cleanse the cups.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: No! stay and talk with me.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I have duties to perform.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Stay–I command you, slave!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I am no slave! your hostage, but no slave.
I go to cleanse the cups.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ho! here's a self–willed thing–here is a spirit !
'I will not, I am no slave! I have duties to perform!
Take me for hostage!' and she flung back her head
As though she brought with her a ton of gold!
`I'll weep no more'–Aha! an impudent thing,
She pleases me! I love to be opposed ;–
I love my horse when he rears, my dogs when they snarl,
The mountain torrent, and the sea, when it flings
Its foam up to the stars:–such things as these
Fill me with life and joy. Tame indolence
Is living death! the battle of the strong
Alone is life!
sp.stage: [During this speech, Parthenia has returned with the cups, and a bundle of field flowers. She seats herself on a piece of rock in front.
sp.p: Ah! she is here again. [He approaches her, and leans over her on the rock.] What art thou making there?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I? Garlands.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Garlands?
sp.l: It seems to me as I before had seen her
In a dream! How! Ah, my brother !–he who died
A child–yes, that is it. My little Folko–
She has his dark brown hair, his sparkling eye;
Even the voice seems known again to me:
I'll not to sleep–I'll talk to her.
These you call garlands,
And wherefore do you weave them?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: For these cups.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Is it not with you a custom? With us
At home, we love to intertwine with flowers
Our cups and goblets.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: What use is such a plaything?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Use?–They are beautiful; that is their use.
The sight of them makes glad the eye; their scent
Refreshes, cheers. ––There.
sp.stage: [Fastens the half–finished garland round a cup, and presents it to him.]
sp.p: Is not that, now, beautiful?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ay–by the bright sun! That dark green mix'd up
With the gay flowers!–Thou must teach our women
To weave such garlands.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: That is soon done: thy wife
Herself shall soon weave wreaths as well as I.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: My wife! my wife !–a woman, dost thou say?
I thank the gods, not I. This is my wife–
My spear, my shield, my sword:–let him who will
Waste cattle, slaves, or gold, to buy a woman;
Not I–not I!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: To buy a woman–how?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: What is the matter? why dost look so strangely ?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: How! did I hear aright? bargain for brides
As you would slaves–buy them like cattle ?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Well, I think a woman fit only for a slave.
We follow our own customs, as you yours.
How do you in your city there?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Consult our hearts.
Massilia's free–born daughters are not sold,
But bound by choice with bands as light and sweet
As these I hold. Love only buys us there.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Marry for love–what! do you love your husbands?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why marry else?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Marry for love; that's strange!
I cannot comprehend. –I love my horse,
My dogs, my brave companions–but no woman !
What dost thou mean by love–what is it, girl?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: What is it? – 'Tis of all things the most sweet–
The heaven of life, –or so my mother says;
I never felt it.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Never?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: No, indeed.
sp.l: Now look how beautiful! – Here would I weave
Red flowers if I had them.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Yonder there,
In that thick wood, they grow.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: How sayest thou?
Oh, what a lovely red !–Go, pluck me some.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I go for thee! the master serve the slave!
sp.p: And yet, why not? I'll go–the poor child's tired.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Dost thou hesitate?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: No, thou shalt have the flowers,
As fresh and dewy as the bush affords,

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I never yet succeeded half so well.
It will be charming!–Charming? and for whom?
Here among savages! no mother here
Looks smiling on it–I am alone, forsaken!
But no, I'll weep no more! No, none shall say I fear !

div.stage: Re–enter Ingomar, with a bunch of flowers, and slowly advancing towards Parthenia.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: The little Folko, when in his play he wanted
Flowers or fruit, would so cry–' Bring them to me;
Quick! I will have them–these will I have or none;'–
Till somehow he compelled me to obey him,–
And she, with the same spirit, the same fire–
Yes, there is much of the bright child in her;
Well, she shall be a little brother to me!
There are the flowers.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Thanks, thanks. Oh, thou hast broke them
Too short off in the stem.
sp.stage: [She throws some of them on the ground.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Shall I go and get thee more?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: No, these will do.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Tell me now about your home–I will sit here,
Near thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Not there: thou art crushing all the flowers.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Well, well; I will sit here, then. –And now tell me,
What is your name!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Parthenia.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Parthenia!
A pretty name!––And now, Parthenia, tell me
How that which you call love grows in the soul;
And what love is: 'tis strange, but in that word
There's something seems like yonder ocean–fathomless.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: How shall I say? Love comes, my mother says,
Like flowers in the night–reach me those violets–
It is a flame a single look will kindle,
But not an ocean quench.
Foster'd by dreams, excited by each thought,
Love is a star from heaven, that points the way
And leads us to its home–a little spot
In earth's dry desert, where the soul may rest–
A grain of gold in the dull sand of life––
A foretaste of Elysium; for when,
Weary of this world's woes, th' immortal gods
Flew to the skies, with all their richest gifts,
Love stayed behind, self–exiled for man's sake!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I never yet heard aught so beautiful!
But still I comprehend it not.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Nor I:
For I have never felt it; yet I know
A song my mother sang, an ancient song,
That plainly speaks of love, at least to me.
How goes it? stay–
'What love is, if thou wouldst be taught,
Thy heart must teach alone, –
Two souls with but a single thought,
Two hearts that beat as one."
'And whence comes love?–Like morning's lignt,
It comes without thy call ;–
And how dies love?–A spirit bright,
Love never dies at all!
And when–and when–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Go on.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I know no more.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Try–try.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I cannot now; but at some other time
I may remember.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Now. –go on, I say.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Not now, I want more roses for my wreath.
Yonder they grow, I will fetch them for myself.
Take care of all my flowers and the wreath !
sp.stage: [Throws the flowers into Ingomar's lap, and runs off.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.stage: [After a pause, without changing his position, speaking to himself in deep abstraction.]
sp.l: 'Two souls with but a single thought,
Two hearts that beat as one.'

div.head: SCENE I.– As before.
div.stage: Enter Alastor, Ambivar, Trinobantes, Samo, and other Alemanni, R. and L.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.p: Well, Alastor, and what says he?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.p: Oh, the old reply—still, still to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Thunder and lightning! thus to linger here! If we join them not soon, those at home will begin the war against the Allobrogi without us and deny us all share of the spoil. Why not choose another chief? Ingomar has become a woman: he leaves the chase and our company, to loll on the grass with this Greek girl, hearing her tales and songs. I say, choose another chief—I'll lead you.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.p: No, no chief but Ingomar. Let us but get this girl away, and he will be himself again.

sp.speaker: Samo.
sp.p: But she is his.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.p: Not so:—she is ours as much; but what shall we do with her?

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.p: Sell her for a slave to the merchants from Carthage. Now on the far off sea a ship of theirs appears. Let us look out, and hail them; then seize the girl, and sell her to them. They will give us arms and armlets for her.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.p: Silence—he is here; —one trial more: away with you.

div.stage: [Exeunt all but Alastor, L.
Enter Ingomar slowly, R. U. E.

lg.l: Home, home! — Ay, to their home, but not to mine,
For here appears my home! It seems to me
As here I was born, —as here my eyes first saw
The light, my heart first felt, my soul first thought.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.p: Now, Ingomar, once more we ask of thee, when wilt thou break the camp up, and return? Thou hearest me not.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Oh, ah! Alastor—yes! thou camest to tell me the fish are all exhausted from the brook; the wild beasts scared from the forests; and there is scarcely food left sufficient for the cattle.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.p: It is so. Nor is that all: the time approaches when our people at home, to avenge the old insult, have resolved upon an inroad on the Allobrogi; and shall we miss it?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Miss it! I?—Ingomar? Thunder and lightning Shall sooner fail the storm than I the strife! the war! — Where are the others?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.p: Encamped yonder upon the moss, waiting your orders.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Give them mead so long as the stock lasts, and let them drink.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.p: What, do we not break up?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: I will consider of it till to-morrow.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.p: Again to-morrow!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Yes, to-morrow, I said.—Go!

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.p: Changed thou seemest to me in word and nature, and scarcely now I know thee.—Well, then, to-morrow.

div.stage: [Exit, L.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Scarce know me! true—I scarcely know myself.
What ails me? — am I ill, then? Yes, that is it.
I am bewildered in a feverish dream;
And my thoughts ramble to I know not where.

div.stage: [Throws himself on a fragment of rock—after a pause.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I struck a roe once with my arrow, while
Close by my victim's side, who soaked the turf
Around her with her blood, her young one stood,
Ignorant of its danger:—as I drew near,
To take up the dead mother on my shoulder,
The fawn sprang to me, and even took its food
Out of my hand, looking up in my face,
With its dark innocent eyes.—'Tis strange, I ever
Think of those eyes when I behold that girl's,—
Now sparkling in their pride, now bright in confidence,
As carelessly she lets her soul appear—
Her childlike soul.
What? She—and she again, and always she!
By all the gods, has Ingomar nothing better
To think of than a woman and her looks:
Than a slave's eyes?
sp.stage: [Clashing of arms, and shouts heard without
sp.l: Hark! how, amid their revelry,
They raise the battle-cry. The clang of arms,
And war, and victory, for me!—Away
With idle dreams! Why, what to me are women?
Yet she—ah! she is not like those at home,
Clad in their shaggy skins, sunburn'd, their bodies
Loaded with clumsy ornaments, happy in bondage,
With base caresses humbly seeking favour
Of their coarse lords. But she—
That cry again !
In vain, in vain! no echo answers you,
Among the pulses of my heart. I–oh, I am sick!
What ails me? Yes, I am ill–sick.

div.stage: Enter Parthenia, L., with a little basket on her arm.– She advances without observing Ingomar.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: My tender father, my poor mother, now
Think on their child: they fancy me, perhaps,
Tormented, ill–used, dead. But how much better
Has it fared with me than I could have dared
To hope! These men are wild, indeed, and rough,
But yet not cruel. And for Ingomar,
He is kind and gentle; yet, at times, how fierce
He looks! as if he'd kill me. [Looking around.] Ah! he is here.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Thou! from whence comest thou?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I have been picking berries
In yonder wood; –see, here is a basket full.
Wilt thou–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: No, no!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No, no!' No, thank you, I think,
Were quite as easily said as 'no !'–no, thank you–
Dost hear? Why dost thou gaze upon me thus?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Away! leave me I would be alone. [Parthenia turns to depart.] No, stay!
Stay with me, Parthenia.
Oh, that thou wert a man!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: A man!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Oh, then would all be right, and happy? Ay,
Thou shouldst be my companion in the chase,
My brother in arms; and I would be to thee
Like to thy shadow, I would watch o'er thee
Whilst thou wert sleeping–would refresh thee
When thou wert weary. As the sea reflects
The heavens, or as the brook the bright blue flowers
That blow upon its banks, so would my soul
Mirror each thought of thine! Thy smiles were mine
Thy griefs, too, mine. Oh! we would share together All things in life.
Two souls with but a single thought,
Two hearts that beat as one."

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Why, that is the old song my mother taught me.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: That is the song that burns into my brain–
The lightning that illuminates the clouds !
Didst thou not tell me once, love was a fire
That a look kindles, and that dreams do foster?
Yes, it is true: –it maddens here; and high,
High as the heaven, rises its flame.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: What, love!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Love, thou didst tell me, did thy mother say,
Love was a star to lead us on to heaven.–
Come, then, oh come! its rays glitter before us,
And bright, and clear, they light us on our way.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: How his eyes sparkle, his cheeks glow! ye gods!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Let the gods rest in the bosom of the clouds;
Let them take with them still whate'er the world
Possessed of good–love, only love. thou said'st,
They have forgotten, –loving let us be then,
And happy.
sp.stage: [Laying hold of her by the hands.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Away!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thus, thus I seize thee–Parthenia, thou art mine.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ho! stand off–away! Another step, and I lie dead before thee.

div.stage: Drawing her dagger and pointing it to her breast.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Hold, hold! Why do I pause? what terror strikes me?
Am I not Ingomar, and is not she
My slave?
How angrily her eyes gleam on me;
I never feared, yet her eyes make me fear !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh, most unhappy!–lost!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I have frightened thee.
I was too rash. I know, rude is my nature,
And rough my manners;–yet my love––

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Thy love! This is not love! The love whose mystic dream
Has filled my heart and thought, is not a thing
Of insult, injury, as you now show to me.
It is a feeling all unselfish, gentle;
One which exalts, ennobles. If a fire,
It is to warm, to cheer, and comfort, not
To blast and scorch. Away, away; profane not
The sacred name. This may be violence,
Passion, but never love !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Remain, I say !
Know'st who I am?–the chief among my people!
The reputation of my deeds resounds
Throughout these mountains, and I am thy master. Girl–who art thou ?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Who am I? I am Parthenia–
An. armourer's child indeed, but yet a Greek–
Massilia's free–born daughter, nourished
On a pure mother's breast, cradled in the arms
Of beauty and refinement, reared from childhood
In the holy service of our righteous gods !
While thou–thou art the rude forest's outlaw son,
A savage–a barbarian–desolater
Of the fair land–a cattle–stealer. – Know,
That we at home flog thieves, and hang up robbers !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Darest thou–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: And now thou knowest who I am,
And who thou art !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Scorn and derision! scorn
To me! Now then, by all the gods, I'll teach thee
How we treat slaves !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: You tame them with the whip,
With hunger, pain, and thirst. ––But your slaves love not.
They only hate, despise, as I do thee !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Be silent, or–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No! for I scorn, deride thee.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thy life !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Take it !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.stage: [Rushing at her with his sword drawn, and suddenly stopping.]
sp.l: No, no, I cannot; –rage
Inflames my blood–my brain will burst.–
Oh, I could tear the world, myself, in pieces.

div.stage: [Throws himself violently on the ground.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: How is this? his sword lies at my feet, which now
Gleamed threatening at my heart! and he struck down,
And almost senseless !–Was I too harsh with him?
Whence came the sudden rage that filled my breast–
This pride, this arrogance? – Do I see right?
He weeps! Why weepest thou, Ingomar?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I weep? 'Tis false–I do not weep! Despise me! me–
The pride and boast of all my race, the terror
Of mine enemies !–By the bright sun!
sp.stage: [After a pause, looking sternly on her.
sp.l: Depart!
Go, I can do without thee; I can I can.
Depart–thou art free! dost hear? free as myself;
Go to thy home–away, do not delay !
Thy breath infects me with a feverish heat!
Thy sight is poison!–Go, go, go !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: How? Free!
Did he say free ?–and shall again my mother,
My father, open to me their arms? And yet
Can I leave him in anger?–him who made
The yoke of slavery so light to me?
Who now has given me freedom, though in rage?
No, no, I'll wait–he will return, and then
A kind word from my lips perhaps will calm
And soften him. Then with a lightened heart
Shall I return.

div.stage: [She seats herself on a rock, while from behind
Enter Samo, Novio, and Ambivar.

sp.speaker: Samo.
sp.l: Ah! she is alone; the boat approaches the shore; now seize her.

div.stage: Novio and Ambivar advance and take hold of her.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ah! ruffians, what would you?

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: Away with her to the beach.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Villains, unhand me.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: Silence, worm!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ingomar! help! save me, Ingomar!

div.stage: They drag her off.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Who calls there? was it not her voice?

div.stage: Enter Ingomar, R.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ambivar? A sword–a sword.
sp.stage: Seizes the sword which he had before let fall on the ground.
sp.l: Ah! here, villains–hold, hold.

div.stage: [Rushes after them. – After a pause, Parthenia rushes on, and falls on the bank.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Saved! saved!

div.stage: Enter Ingomar, hurriedly, L.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.stage: [Going up to Parthenia, and taking her hand.
sp.l: It is I–I–how white thou art!
Thou tremblest; art thou hurt? Parthenia,
It is my arm supports thee. Did they dare
With their rough hands to seize my lovely flower?
Why dost thou tremble? Oh! they shall repent it:
They shall, like worms, crawl in the dust before thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Hark, steps–they come.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Fear not, for I am with thee.
No power on earth shall harm thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Look–they come.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Let them! Like the eagle when its nest is seized,
With god–like strength I feel my arm is braced;
And if Heaven's lightning strike me not, I bid
Defiance to all power man can bring.

div.stage: Enter the Alemanni, Alastor, Novio, and Samo, L.U.E., armed with spears, swords, and clubs.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Stand off, and speak! What brings you?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: Thou hast wounded Ambivar to the death.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: That did I when he dared to seize upon
This maid, my property.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: She is not thine.

sp.speaker: Samo.
sp.l: Give up the woman.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Sooner my life.

sp.speaker: Nov.
sp.l: Seize her.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Come on.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: They are too many–they will kill thee !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Away, woman!–come on.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: Hold–hear me, friends; and hear me, Ingomar.
We chose thee for our leader, and we promised thee
The fifth part of the booty. But thou givest
Thyself to indolent rest, and proudly dost
Appropriate this slave. Thus thou hast broken
The laws of right and peace.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I broke them not. 'Twas he, that other, did,
Who, seizing her, robbed you as well as me,
And well deserved his fate. But I am weary
Of holding your proud race in check. Then go:–
Choose your own path. I separate myself
From you. But she is mine. –The fifth of the spoil,
My share by right, I give you as her ransom.
Is it agreed? If not, then let the sword–––

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: The fifth of the spoil! said he so, indeed?

sp.speaker: Samo.
sp.l: Shall we agree?

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: The fifth of the booty, didst thou say?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I did.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: Then be it so. – The slave is thine.
But still, if thou wilt lead our steps towards home,
We will obey thee as truly as before.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: No, I am weary–I will seek new lands,
New customs. Go you hence–I will remain.

sp.speaker: Alas.
sp.l: Consider the inroad on the Allobrogi.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I have considered all enough.–Farewell.

div.stage: [Exeunt Alemanni, L.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: They are gone. And now, Parthenia, thou art safe–
Thou art free. How pale thou art, and trembling still.
Here, sit thee down and rest.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh, Ingomar,
Be thanked, be blessed !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thanked––and for what?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I know
Thou only didst that which thy generous heart
Compelled thee to; and yet have I, deserted
By my own people, in the desert found
From thee protection.
sp.stage: [She kisses his hand, and bursts into tears.
sp.l: And now–now, ––farewell.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Farewell?–what say'st thou?
Wilt thou not go with me?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Thou hast restored my freedom: I would seek
My home.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I give thee freedom?–I! thou dreamest.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: What! wilt thou break thy word?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: My word! did I give my word?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Thou didst.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Go, go, then–go.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Bless thee!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Stay, stay, Parthenia. Oh! it seems
That day no more shall shine upon the earth,
The sun's bright beams be quenched in endless night.
Parthenia, wilt thou go? oh, wilt thou leave me?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: My parents wait their child.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: They do;–go, go, then !
Yet think of the dark wood, the dizzy cliff,
The dreadful chasms, and the roaring floods,
The wolf and bear–and thou to go alone.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I came alone, and can return so, too.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thou wilt be lost. Alastor, Novio, –––
They shall conduct thee. Ho, there!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: They! oh, no.
Rather the wolves and bears than those wild ruffians.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ah, true, indeed. –That were to trust the lamb
To the wolf's keeping. I, I will myself
Conduct thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Thou?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Why dost thou look so fearful?
Thou thinkest me no safer than the rest.
But now I am not what I was. –Till now
Never did I know fear, scarce tears–not even when
A child. But thou hast taught me both to–day.
Doubt me no more–believe me, trust me, then;
I call the gods to witness––

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Nay, swear not:
Thine eyes speak truer, holier, than oaths;
And if they lie, then all is false indeed !
Conduct me, be my guide–I trust thee.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ah!
Thou dost consent? Oh! I will seek thee out
The forest's coolest shade, the softest turf,
Guard thee from every stone, from every brier;
My arm shall thus support–no, not support–
But carry thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Dost think I am a child,
That thou wouldst carry me? I do not want
Even thine arm–I care not for fatigue–
Thou shalt not carry me: but–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: The basket.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: The basket ?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Yes, the basket with the berries.
Wilt thou not do it?
sp.stage: [Taking up a basket from the ground, and handing it to him.]

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Yes, I will–I will.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: And I will take thy spear, thy shield, and sword.
sp.stage: [Taking them from the tree against which Ingomar had placed them.]

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: No, no, that cannot be.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: It shall be so, –
It is my humour. From my childhood up,
You know, I have been accustomed to bright arms;
I seem to inherit it even in my blood,
From my dear father. And now, why delay we?
Thou hast the basket, I the arms, we'll go.
Dost hear? Why standest thou silent–motionless?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: All seems a dream to me. Come, then, this way–
Down by the rock.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Forward! the guide before.
I will close follow thee–my friend, protector:on

div.head: Scene I.
div.stage: In the background appears Massilia, and a view of the Sea. In the front, to the left, a rocky eminence overgrown with bushes, from which a narrow path leads down to the stage.
Enter Myron, Adrastus, and Elphenor, L.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: Shame, I say, shame! The wolf will help the wolf, yet yonder town, that boasts its civilization, justice, and law, sees, without stirring a hand, her citizens become a prey to slavery, and is deaf to her children's cry for help. Shame, I say–shame!

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Full well thou know'st 'tis an old law, first made when the infant colony struggled for existence with the wild natives of the land, that no further than the shadow of her walls reached would the state protect her citizens;–and thee they seized in the mountains.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: Oh, wise decree! Oh, father–like protection! First they refuse a child her parent's ransom; and when she, following her heart's pious bent, submits her own head to the yoke for mine, then they deny me aid, in men or money, to rescue my poor child from worse than death – Again I cry shame–shame!

sp.speaker: Elp.
sp.p: We are not strangers to your grief, but suffer with you; and when thy child asked us for help, we paused, only to find a path of deliverance, while she–

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: Ah, she! a woman in heart, a man in courage !– Oh, my poor child–my child !

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Thou knowest Lykon, the fisherman, who brought the news of thy capture, has summoned us for counsel, help, and hope; and if the men of the coast join with our friends within Massilia, thy child may yet be rescued. See, here comes Lykon; and with him those who look like friends.

div.stage: Enter Lykon, surrounded and followed by Women and Fishermen.

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.p: Where is Myron? which is he? which is the brave girl's father?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: Here, here.–––And will you help us? will you save my child?

sp.speaker: Fish.
sp.p: Ay, ay, we'll do our best.

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.p: Though ourselves natives of the soil, we hate the Alemanni, and respect the Greeks. Besides, it would dis– grace Massilia, and Greece itself, should such a pious daughter and brave maid be lost. All that we can we'll give.

sp.speaker: Women.
sp.p: Yes, yes–our ornaments, our prayers.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: Bless you! the gods repay you! But we must not lose a day, as the wild people will soon return further up the mountains, and my child will be dragged to slavery or death.

sp.speaker: Lyk.
sp.p: We will disperse through the villages, and rouse the young–ay, and the old–to the rescue. You, Adrastus, to the right–I to the left. Meanwhile you, Myron, and Elphenor, seek the house of the old Rhesus; he is rich, and has promised aid. Await my coming there. And now, my friends, away, away.

div.stage: [Exeunt Fishermen, Women, &c.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: My child, my child! shall I again behold thee? did not age stiffen my limbs, I would myself–

sp.speaker: Elp.
sp.p: Come, come, let us to the house of the wealthy Rhesus.

div.stage: Parthenia and Ingomar appear on the cliff, L.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Here, here, Parthenia, this way–by this path.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No, yonder is the way–down there.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Hold, hold! that is to danger–see you not?
This way–give me thy hand.

div.stage: [They descend the path on to the stage

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: When wilt thou trust me?
Hast thou forgotten yesterday, the moor
Where, following thine own will, the ground gave way
Beneath thy feet, and if I had not then
From off my arm thrown my broad shield, whose face,
Upheld thy failing steps–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I should have sunk!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: And I with thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I think thou wouldst ! Yes, yes,
I was preserved from death, and by thine arms;
Thy shield lies in the morass, –and last night, too,
Under the bank, whose turf and moss afforded
But scanty firing, thou didst break thy spear,
And with its fragments make a cheerful blaze,
To warm and comfort me. Oh, thou true guide!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Then come–this way.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: It seems as if that path–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Again! Why, look, the wood is ended here.
And the mountain grows more level

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ah! thou art right–the forest spreads behind us:
It seems to me I ought to know this place.
Was it not here that, when I left my home
To seek my father, on my knees I prayed
The gods for courage, strength, and victory?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ah! say not so. Far, far from here I'd have
Thy home.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Yes, here it was.

div.stage: [She turns to the background and recognizes Massilia.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ah! and behold, there rolls the sea;
And yonder, shining in the purple light,
Appears Artemis' temple. Oh, Massilia!
My home, my home! again I throw myself
Upon the earth, with thanks, with gratitude.
Immortal gods, who have watched my lonely path,
The work of love is done, and safely back
You bring me home again. Oh, thanks and praise!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Would that I lay beside my shield in the morass.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.stage: [Rising and coming forward, accompanied by Ingomar.]
sp.l: My father, mother, I shall see them again;
Weeping with joy, shall sink into their arms,
And kiss the falling tears from their pale cheeks.
Oh! be saluted by me, my native city !
See how the evening light plays on each column,
Each wall, and tower, like the smile of a god.
Look, Ingomar, is it not glorious?
What ails thee? why art thou now grown sulky
Like a vexed child, when joy lends my soul wings?
Didst thou endure with me the burning sun,
The frost of night, and the rough path, and now
Wilt not rejoice, –now that our toil is over?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I–I rejoice?
In the dark forest, the bleak wilderness,
Alone with thee, the heavens above, around us
Loneliness and deep silence, there–yes, there
Where fear and danger pressed thee to my side
Did I rejoice; I was thy world. But here,
Where those accursed walls throw their cold shades,
To tear our souls assunder–here–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ah me!
Yes, I remember––here we part.–And yet
Not here–come with me to the city.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I?
Yonder, with polished Greeks, caged in dark walls?
I the barbarian, the free man! No, yonder
Thy pathway lies–this to my mountain home.
Oh! would that I had never seen thee, girl!
Enough–farewell!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: No, stay;–thou shalt not go Without one gift, that in some distant time May call again my image to thy memory. Take this.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thy dagger! Is it to remind me
How once my violence armed thine own hand with it
Against thyself?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No: to remind thee how
Two days and nights, alone, through moor and wood
And briery thicket, thou didst still protect me,
Guard me, and guide without my needing once
To touch its hilt. – Of this let it remind thee.
