And so, [Hesitating.] farewell !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: No, no! I cannot, will not–
Oh, do not leave me! be my own, Parthenia;
Oh, be my wife ! I am chief among my people;
Plenty dwells in my tent at home; fear not
That aught of our rough manners shall offend thee;
Follow thy native customs there as freely
As I. Thou shalt be mistress of thyself,
Of all, our queen! Oh, come, then–I will build
A home for thee in the shadow of the trees.–
Before us a rich meadow with its herds,
Beside, a stream, around all green and still,
While the soft evening air breathes through the open door,
And melts our hearts to love and happiness :
Say yes–say yes–and come where joy and bliss
Shall ever reign.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ah me!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Why dost thou droop thine eyes? why art thou silent?
Thou canst not doubt me–thou thyself didst tell me,
True love was gentle, meek, unselfish, tender.
By yonder heaven, such will I be to thee.
Oh, I will hold thee with as tender bonds
As thine own hand the wreath thou weav'st; will see
Each wish told in thine eyes, ere thou hast thought it;
Whatever lives in earth, in sea, in air,
Shall minister to thy desires. Rich shalt thou be,
Honoured, and happy.–Oh, then, doubt no more!
Be mine–be mine, and speak no more of parting.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Hush–hush this syren song!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thou wilt not?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Listen.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Oh, thou believest me not–thou hatest me!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No–I respect–honour–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: But canst not love.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: My parents–Think, can I desert their age?–
Forget long years of love and care–resign
The worship of the gods–the quiet customs
Of my own home, to follow, among strangers, My country's foe?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I know it–thou despisest me.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No, by my life ! I hold thee for most noble,
Most good! a bright and glorious star, but shadowed
By a light cloud, –a cup of ruby wine,
With the wreath only wanting.
Wert thou a Greek;
Were right, law, order, not unknown to thee;
Were violence not thy god, the sword thy judge;
Wert thou not a––

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Why pause? Yes, speak it :
Barbarian! that am I called–a cattle–stealer–
Yes, I remember well! 'twas thine own word ;–
A desolater–an assassin !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ingomar!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I see it all. There is a gulf indeed
Between us, and thou art ashamed of me.
Thou fearest the jeer of thy refin'd companions:
The polished Greeks would mock at the rough savage.
Thou art right; I should but shame–disgrace thee.
Yes, thou art right; – farewell.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh, leave me not in anger.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: In anger! Oh, Parthenia, couldst thou
But see this heart! I–I–No more–farewell.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ingomar! stay, hear me! He heeds me not;
He flies up the steep cliff; he is gone, and I
Shall never see him more! Why, how is this?
What sudden change has come upon the world?
How green, how bright, was all before: and now
How dim and dark the twilight grows! How faded
The grass, how dry the leaves! It seems to me
As if the young spring were about to die.[Weeps.
What! tears? I must not weep; no, no, I must not.
Rouse thee, Parthenia, –thou hast duties. Think,
Thy home awaits thee–parents, friends, companions.
Oh, Ingomar! whom shall I find there like to thee?
Thou good, thou generous one! Lost–lost! [Weeps.

div.stage: Ingomar re–enters, and slowly approaches.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Parthenia!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ah! come back again !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I am: I cannot, will not leave thee.
I will go with thee to the city;–I–
I will become a Greek !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: How sayest thou ?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thou dost not despise me, Parthenia–no,
Thou art not ashamed of me, but only of
My nation, my rough ways:––––there's remedy
For that, it can be mended. Though I am
No Greek, yet I am a man, for 'tis the soul
That makes the man, and not his outward seeming;
My shield and spear are left in the morass,
So will I leave my nation, manners, all,
To follow thee. In yonder town, for thee
I will become a Greek.––And now I've said it,
I am strong and well again.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Thou'lt follow me?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I know I've much to learn, but thou wilt teach me;
And that will make all easy. When 'tis done,
Thou'lt love me then! thou wilt–I feel it here–
Ay, like a sunbeam in my heart it glows;
It shouts like the loud triumph of a conqueror ;
Like the voice of the high gods, it penetrates
My soul: thou'lt love me then! thou'lt love me then!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: If not, oh heaven! whom can I ever love?
Thou'lt follow me to Massilia. But, unknown,
Where wilt thou find a host to give thee shelter?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: A host? – The first that comes across my path
I'll ask for salt and fire. What needs there more?
And see, already two approach, who look [Looking off, R.
Like Greeks. Them will I–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ah! 'tis he–'tis he–my father!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Her father! the gods smile upon me, then,
And lead him here as my appointed friend.

div.stage: Re–enter Parthenia, with Myron and Elphenor.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: My darling child restored to me!–Oh, let me
Bless the brave man who–
Ah! what do I see?
Elphenor–help! The Alemanni–fly!

div.stage: Ingomar turns.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Fear not! 'twas he himself, 'twas Ingomar,
Who gave thy child her freedom, and who now
Brings her in safety to thine arms again.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: What say'st thou?–he? and he, he came alone?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: He comes a friend, a suppliant to thee;
And oh! be kind to him, as he has been
To me. Hear him, my father; [Leads Ingomar to him.]
And now, Elpenor,
My mother–tell me of her.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: He is really come alone!–Then I suppose
All's safe. Hesitatingly to Ingomar. I thank thee–thou art welcome–very!
I did not think to see you again so soon–
You are come about the ransom.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Bah!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Do not be angry: I have not got it yet ;–
But a few drachmas, but I'll give you those.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Old man, your ransom's paid: I bought it, with
Your child's release, at the cost of all I owned;–
I give you both.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: You!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Now I ask your friendship, and come to live with you.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: To live with me! You! one of the Alemanni.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Well, I have been
Your enemy, I own it!–made you my prisoner,
True!–treated you as my slave, agreed !–but yet
I have done you service, too, and come in peace.
Let all be blotted out !––––There is my hand–
Accept it, and you'll find me, perhaps, more true
As friend than enemy. Do you fear to take it?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Fear? n–n–no. Greeks never fear;–
But you are quite sure you have come alone?
No: I don't fear you, but the citizens–
If they–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Tell them that Ingomar comes single
Into the midst of them, to ask a home.
If any bear him malice for past wrongs,
Let them stand forth. Say Ingomar is here,
To answer one and all.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Merciful powers, he'd challenge the whole city !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I have little thought for them. But thou, old man,
I'd have thee be my friend–ay, more, my father.
Give me thy hand as to thy son. [Myron reluctantly does so.
That's well.
Now take me to thy roof, and teach me thy customs;
Teach me among the Greeks a Greek to be.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: I take thee to my house !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: It shall be sacred
As the temple of a god.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Thou learn to be a Greek! and learn from me, too!
I–I–I know I'm bound to you for much,
For many thanks: but a poor man am I;
And shouldst thou be my guest, thou needs must share
Poverty with us, weariness, and care,
Complying with our household customs.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Poverty!
I have given up my race and home. Then tell me,
Can I be poorer? Weariness and care!
Can these be where Parthenia dwells? Out, out,
Old man! you do but mock me: tell me, rather,
What must I do?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Why, first, strip off thy skin.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: My skin! Oh, this?
sp.stage: [Looking at the skin thrown over his shoulder.]
sp.l: Ha! ha! Well, be it so.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: And then thou must cut short thy hair and beard.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: My hair and beard! That will I never! they
Are my proud race's mark of free descent,
Growing freely with the free.
sp.stage: [Turning, and his eyes meeting those of Parthenia.]
sp.l: And yet–well, well,
I will cut them off.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: How wondrous tame he grows !
He that was wild as an unbroken horse.
Then I have fields up yonder, on the hills;
A vineyard, also ;–work must there be done, too,
With plough and harrow; and thou–––

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: What! guide the plough and harrow!
Root up the earth like ants and moles ! Slaves only
Guide ploughs; and wilt thou make of me a slave?
By the loud thunder–

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Be calm, calm. Remember, 'twas thyself
Did wish to be a Greek, and we are poor.
We all must work–not I alone: my wife ;
Parthenia, too–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Parthenia, didst thou say?
Parthenia labour ?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Ay, why not? She, too, must–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: She? Parthenia? No, that shall she never!
I'll work for her at any toil you will;
The plough, the harrow, anything. What more?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: And then, too, thou must help me at my forge.
And learn how to make arms.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ay, by my life,
That will I joyfully! that must be glorious !
That's spending strength on strength; the hammer thrashing
The shrieking steel, that writhes to every blow!
Ay, that is brave, that's noble! By my life,
Making good swords must almost be as pleasant
As wielding them.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Stay–stay! Thou must not wield them:
We are a quiet people, and love peace;
And therefore thou must give up thy sword.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: My sword!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: It is forbidden, under heavy penalties,
For strangers to go armed into Massilia.
I will take care of it for thee. – Give it to me.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: My father's sword! that which has given me
Defence and victory! Give me up my sword!
Thou art playing with my softness, to insult me.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Parthenia.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Give thee this sword? sooner my blood–my life !
My sword's myself–the sword and man are one.
Bid any come and take it, if he dare.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ingomar, thou wilt give thy sword to me.
Dost thou remember how I carried it
From the mountain? You will trust me with it now.
sp.stage: [He lets her gently disengage it from his hand.
sp.l: Father, haste on before. I long to embrace
My mother. Go, prepare her–we will follow thee.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Wonderful! Elpenor, go thank the fishermen,
And tell them all. Give up his sword! oh, marvel!

div.stage: [Exit, R.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Why dost thou linger, Ingomar?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Who's he?
Who spoke of Ingomar? dost thou mean me?
Am I, then, Ingomar? My senses whirl;
Beneath my feet the solid earth seems falling.
I am a child–a fool–I will not! Stay!
Give me my sword again !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Come, Ingomar!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Parthenia!

div.stage: [Rushes out, R.

div.head: SCENE –Same as in Act 1.
div.stage: Enter Elphenor, from Myron's house L.

sp.speaker: Elp.
sp.p: Come, what delays thee, Myron ? they wait for thee.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.stage: Appearing on the steps in the act of arranging his dress.
sp.p: I will be ready in an instant. I but take off my sooty working coat, fit to appear before the council. Actea, quick–my girdle, and my cloak.

div.stage: Enter Actea, followed by Polydor, L.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.stage: [Coming forward with Myron's girdle in her hand.]
sp.p: What can they want with you at the council?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: Want Myron at the council! I'll stay and listen; I may gain some profit out of it.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: What do they want me for? No doubt, an order for a large supply of arms. They find that none can make so well as Myron, especially now Ingomar assists me.

sp.speaker: Elp.
sp.p: Quick,–see, another messenger.

div.stage: Enter Neocles, L.

sp.speaker: Neo.
sp.p: Myron, the Timarch is impatient: all is confusion at the council.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: Confusion? What is it, then?

sp.speaker: Neo.
sp.p: The gates are closed, the guards are doubled.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: What is the matter?

sp.speaker: Neo.
sp.p: How, have you not heard? We are surrounded by the Alemanni; the hills about the city swarm with them; and loudly at the council they call for Myron.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Ye gods, 'tis as I feared, then ; I said he was a spy, a traitor.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: Aha! I taught her that!

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: A traitor saidst thou, who?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: 'Twas not for nothing that the flames crackled when he entered our house, and that the raven croaked; they warned us, yet in vain.

sp.speaker: Neo.
sp.p: Whom do you mean? Who is a spy, a traitor?

div.stage: Enter Parthenia, from house.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Who? who but Ingomar?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Who dares call Ingomar a spy?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: I, thy mother.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: Hold your tongue, you are a fool

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Polydor says it, too,

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: Polydor is another fool, then.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: Is he, indeed? I'll make you treat him, though, with more respect ere long !

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.p: It is the weak alone are traitors, and Ingomar is very Hercules: any one who saw him at the plough, the anvil, or the games, would need no more to swear him a true man. Why, my earnings are trebled since Ingomar worked with me. [Taking the girdle from Actea and completing his toilet by putting it on.] There–now I am ready, be not alarmed. No doubt, the council summon me for my opinion. I know the Alemanni–I have been among them, and I fear them not, –I've proved that. Come, come.

div.stage: Exit, followed by Neocles, L.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: The foe at our gates! he summoned to the council. If they should, instead of asking his opinion, bring him for his folly to a reckoning, perhaps to punishment?–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Fear not, mother: the fathers knew of Ingomar, and gave permission to receive him.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: He has brought mischief on our house.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Mother, he brought thy child in safety back there.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Well, well; and so he did. But Polydor says truly–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Mother, mother, why will you give your ear to that malicious wretch ?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: That's me!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why suffer him to turn your heart against the noblest––

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Bah! I tell you, Polydor–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I will not hear his name! Why will he still pursue me? why you still urge for him? I tell you, mother, were beggary and death set for my choice, I would embrace them sooner than that detested man!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: You would? you shall, then !–I'll bring down that proud spirit, though it should cost me half my means.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: But, child, he threatens us–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: He threatens! the cold dastard–let him! I spurn his threats as I do him.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: I'll hear no more: I'll go at once and do it, cost me what it may!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: He dares to threaten !

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: Tremble !

div.stage: [Exit, L.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p:
Hush! If he should hear you. I'm sure I don't know why you hate him so. At least, he never drew his sword on you, as Ingomar once did, he never took your
father for a slave, as Ingomar– O, how I hated him as soon as I set my eyes upon him. His very look, and that long hair, and his rough and wiry beard. Ugh! he made my heart sick !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Yet he now wears both short, and like a Greek.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: The very children in the street called after him Faun, and Satyr.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: But thou knowest he goes, now, clad like others.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Ay! Greek may be his coat and mantle; but his bearing, walk, and voice–the fixed disdain in his mien and look and speech, these all are the barbarian's still, and will remain so. Ever his forest nature clings to him.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why should it not, when freedom, courage, and strength, like his own forests, animate his soul?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: The rough strength of a bear! Did not he yesterday, at the games, throw his adversary right out of the circle; did he not fling the quoit so far, he nearly struck the Timarch.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Did he not, too, destroy the wolf that had so long ravaged our fields? and in the harbour, when Lysippus' boat struggled with the storm, who sprang into the boiling waves, and dragged him safe to shore but Ingomar? and who but he relieves from the forge and the plough my gray–haired father?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Well, well, perhaps he does. He may have some good in him; but he pays no respect to me and I say again he is a spy, a traitor, and so I'll tell him to his face. Where is he? [Calls.] Ingomar !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Stay, mother, stay! what would you do? Respect, at least, the rights of a guest.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: What, Ingomar, I say! Yes, thou shalt see how he will shrink and tremble, when I tell him that I know him,–Ingomar!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Mother! how little dost thou know of that pure soul, that noble heart.

div.stage: Enter Ingomar, from back of stage, dressed in the costume of a Greek Peasant.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Who called me ?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: So, thou art come at last. Thrice must I call?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: I was preparing for the evening sports, and singing.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Singing! Yes, for joy to meet your friends again.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: What friends ?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Oh, you don't know, not you, that the Alemanni surround the city.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Indeed! They come this way, then, in their Incursion on the Allobrogi ?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: The Allobrogi! oh, how innocent! But be their road, sir, where it may, there are some people think, hint, –ay, and maintain, their way and yours are one.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Their way and mine!

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Ay; who even say that you have introduced yourself here, only to open doors and gates to them.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: I–who says that?

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: I say so, to thy face–that thou art a spy, a traitor–that thou art–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: Woman! [Then checks himself] But no, no, no, thou art Parthenia's mother–I will not answer thee.

div.stage: [Abruptly walks into the house.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Look, he derides my anger. He does not think it worth his trouble to justify himself to me! he dares–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.stage: [Goes up to the house, and calls.]
sp.p: Ingomar !

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: Why do you call him? Shall he again affront me?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: No, he shall answer.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.p: I will have no answer–you'll drive me mad, among you! There is thy father–danger perhaps threatens his very life; I'll follow him to the council; thou mayst stay and ask for answers from this proud barbarian, and thou mayst trust him, too; but, for me, I know him! and me he never shall deceive.

div.stage: Exit, L.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: She is wrong,
She is very wrong, and he bears all the blame.
Poor Ingomar !

div.stage: [Turns and sees Ingomar slowly descending the steps –she beckons him.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Come here. Dost think
Thou hast treated with respect my mother, Myron's wife,
To turn thy back on her, and walk away
Without an answer?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Didst thou not bid me, when thy mother might,
As age will do, find fault without a cause,
I should be silent then, and go away?
She did find fault with me without a cause,
So I said nothing, and I went away.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: But couldst thou not look gentle and speak thus–
'No, thou art wrong, I am no spy, no traitor.'
But thou, instead, must fly into a rage,
And leave me to bear all the pain.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.p: I am sorry.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I cannot make you heed my words, and never–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Not heed thy words! I think of nothing eise:
Labouring or resting, at the plough, the anvil,
In very sleep, still I repeat your lessons.
But all in vain! Oh, I shall never learn
And thou wilt never love me!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Nay, thou hast
Learn'd much already, and–

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Oh, my wild woods,
My mountain home! There the heart speaks its will.
And the free act is open as the thought.
'Tis thus I have grown up–I cannot change it.
What moves me,–love or hate, pleasure or pain,–
Breaks from my lips, shows in my looks, and sparkles
From out my eyes :– I must be what I am, –
I can be nothing else!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Nor shalt thou be !
I would not have thee other than thou art–
Honest, and pure, and true.
Yet even the candour of a noble soul
Requires restriction. See, thou hast learn'd much :
Thou honourest law and order thou hast left
The bloody service of thy mountain gods,
For the pure worship of my people. See,
Thou art a Greek already in thy heart;
Yet be more gentle, more but that will come.
The sculptor, who, from out of the rough stone,
Would call the image of a god to life,
First learns to smooth the coarse unpolished shell
That shrouds it.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: And then, after I have learn'd,
When I am more what thou desirest, Parthenia,
Wilt thou then–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Stop, thou hast not learn'd it yet.
And wilt not soon.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ah, thus it ever is !
In place of paying the poor scholar's zeal,
Thou dost withdraw the goal still further from me.
Thou art altered, too, thou once didst seek, encourage me,
Didst tell me tales and sing me songs; but now
Thou art distant, cold.–Well, well, I will not weary ther
Content if I can gaze into thine eyes,
And–

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Parthenia–Parthenia !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Hark! my father.

div.stage: Enter Myron, L., followed by Actea.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Parthenia! Ay–and Ingomar, where is he?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Here.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Now, what is it? Will you never tell me?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Stop–give me air, let me breathe first, what do you think?
Know! they are coming, they will be here directly.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Who–the enemy?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: His grace the Timarch!

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Ah! I said so–I said
That Ingomar would bring us no good luck.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Then you talked nonsense, as you always do.
He brings us glory, consideration, honour !
But here they are. Now, Ingomar, dear friend,
Be ready–I go to greet him.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Consideration! honour! how my heart beats!
Like a forge hammer.

div.stage: Enter the Timarch, accompanied by Attendants, Myron receives him with low bows.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Enough, enough–Myron, where is thy guest,
Thy pupil?

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Here, illustrious sir–
Will you step into the house?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: No, call him hither.

div.stage: [Myron beckons Ingomar forward, and he advances towards the Timarch.]

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: So, friend, thy name is Ingomar.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ay–as thou sayest.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Say 'your grace!' Dost thou understand? – your grace.'

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: I hear thou wouldst become a Greek,
Be naturalized–Massilia's citizen.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Such is my wish.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Massilia grants thy wish–
A house within her walls shall be assigned thee;
Added to which, three hydes of land, with the freedom
And the full privileges of a citizen.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: To me–this, this to me!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ye gods !

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Dost hear, wife?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Nay, more;–thou lovest this maid: thirty ounces of silver
Shall her dower be–she shall be thine, thy wife.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Parthenia !

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: So thou prove only that Massilia's welfare
Lies at thy heart, all these shall then be thine.
Say, in return what wilt thou do?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: What do !
What will I not do? I will lift the world
From off its solid centre, drink the ocean,
Tear down the stars from heaven! I am but mad–
Yet all that is possible–ay, or impossible,
I'll do for bliss like this.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Thou hast heard the Alemanni now
Surround the city–they come against us to––

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: No, no, you err. Against the Allobrogi
This expedition moves, not against you–
Not you.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Be as it may, we hold them dangerous,–
Massilia would extirpate them.
Thou knowest them :
Thou shalt go to their camp, as though thou cam'st
To seek thy friends and hear the news of home;
So shalt thou well observe their mode of war,
The approaches of their camp, their watchword, and
The arrangement of their guard. Return in the evening,
And then by night conduct Massilia's soldiers,
And lead them forth to conquest.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ah!

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: What sayest thou?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ensnare,
Betray my countrymen !–deceive the men
Who trust me–murder them in their sleep–
The men who speak my tongue, who were my brothers?

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Think of the reward–Parthenia, honour, riches,

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Take all thy offers back! take even her,
For she is all to me! my heart, my soul,
My life! Yet take her, too: for, had I her,
And all the happiness the earth could give,
It were despair, shame, misery, and death,
To purchase her by baseness such as this.

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Dost thou not wish to be a Greek?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I did,
For then I did not know that Greeks were traitors
I said farewell to mine own kin and nation–
I gave up all to make my home with you,
And had you called on me to fight for you
On the open field of war, I would have stood
Faithfully by you to the death; but [With contempt.] Grecian
Weapons are treachery, cunning, cowardice, –
In these I am unpractised.–Go, go, go!
We do not understand each other–you are civilized,
Refined, and I but a barbarian! Go!

sp.speaker: Tim.
sp.l: Restrain thy bold tongue–one hour for decision
We give thee yet. Refuse, and thy false breath,
No longer shall contaminate our city.
Choose, then !–And thou, Myron, if afterward
Thou or befriend or shelter him, thy life
Shall answer for it!–Back to the council.

div.stage: [Exit Timarch, with Suite.]

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Now, who was right? Where is the honour,
The consideration, that this Ingomar
Was to have brought? – He brings thy head in danger.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: No, not my head !
I will have nothing more to do with him.
Away, depart,–I shut my door against thee:
I am Massilia's true citizen.
Go into the house, Parthenia.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Myron.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Go, go in, wife–in, girl.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: One word.

div.stage: [Actea and Parthenia go into the house.]

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Not one! You see the danger you have brought me.
I owe thee thanks; and, had I two heads, willingly
Would I lose one for thee. But I have but one;
And therefore, go, go, go.– [In a loud voice.] I am a trueman,
And a good citizen–and so, farewell !

div.stage: [Exit into house, shutting the door.]

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: 'Tis past, then! All is over, all is lost.
Never will she be mine. Never again
Shall I behold her face, or hear her voice.
She is lost! Why, then, delay?–Away, away;
And let them close their coward gates upon me.
I'll die, or break a passage through their spears.

div.stage: [Going.
Enter Parthenia, who during his last words comes out of the house, and approaches unperceived.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ingomar! wilt thou go?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Dost doubt it?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Whither?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Ask me not whither;
There are on earth only two paths for me,
One to the heaven where thou art and where
Thou art not, all is there a barren desert
That path is mine. Son of the wilderness,
I bend my steps again towards my mother:
She gave me truth for my inheritance,
And I will keep it, though my heart should burst.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: And thou wilt go?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Wouldst thou desire my stay,
To be dishonoured? Yet thine image still
Shall never leave me–thou, Parthenia
Farewell.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Not yet–not yet.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Quick death is easy, –
He who dies slowly dies a thousand times.
Farewell.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Thy sword–thou hast forgot thy sword:
On entering here, thou gavest it to my father.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: I want it not. Hope took it from my hand;
And now–now–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Yet 'tis here. –Look, I return it,
Bright as when first thou gavest it up.
Not so:
But I will bear it for thee.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thou, Parthenia !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I carried, with it once thy spear and shield;
Then why not now thy sword?

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Oh, then ––But let that pass–let us part here.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No, Ingomar: I will bear thy sword for thee.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Where? to the market?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: No, further to the gate;
Still further to the sea–beyond the sea–
Over the mountains over valleys, floods–
To east and west. – Wherever thy path leads,
Wherever thou dost bend thy wandering steps,
So long as my heart beats, as my pulse throbs,
So long I will go with thee !

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Thou, Parthenia,
Wilt–

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Ay, will follow thee where'er thou goest.
Thy way shall be my way–thy fate be mine.
Where thou dost build thy house, there, too, shall be
My home; the language that sounds on thy lips,
That will I speak; what pleases thee shall be
My joy; and what afflicts thee, that will I
Suffer, too, with thee. Thine am I, and nothing
Shall part us more!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Do I dream? Thou liest on
My breast,–thou lovest me!–thou Massilia's child,
And I the stranger, the barbarian !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Oh, speak that word no more; for what are we,
Compared to thee, thou good, thou noble one!
How they stood shamed before thee! the proud Greeks.
Before thee: who camest here to learn our laws–
But who hast taught to them that holy law
Of truth and honour, which the gods themselves
Impressed upon thy heart!
How great, how glorious thou stood'st bei
When thou for duty gavest up more than life
The hope of life! And, oh, how shamed I feel
That I presumed to teach thee! Pardon me–
Forgive me...

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Parthenia mine! mine!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Long have I been thine ;–
Ay, since the day when thou didst learn to weep and fear.
When from thy hand dropped the uplifted sword,
Which threatened at my life. Yes, since that day
I loved thee; and if in shame I tried to hide it from thee,
I only loved thee more. And did I once
With foolish tyranny lay on thee trials,
And with a vain superiority presume
Upon thy noble nature? let me pay
The penalty of my pride, while thus in love
And humbleness, as wife, as servant, slave,
I sink down in the dust before thy feet.
sp.stage: [She is about to kneel, when Ingomar checks her, and takes her to his bosom.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Before my feet! my slave! No, as two stems
With one root let us be,–springing, twined upwards
Towards the vault of heaven. we will be–
Two souls with but a single thought,
Two hearts that beat as one.'

div.stage: Enter Myron and Actea, from house.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Ah! what do I see? Degenerate girl,
Into the house with thee !

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Not without Ingomar.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Have you not heard the penalty?
Begone!

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Not without her. She is mine, and mine for ever

div.stage: Enter Polydor, with two Greeks, L.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Indeed–perhaps, then, you will pay these bonds?
Two hundred drachmas, or, to speak more closely,
Two hundred and thirteen.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: What means this man?
Good friend, I owe thee naught.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: No, I confess
I have no claim on you–but Myron, there,
And he shall pay me every drachma, too.
Ah! hal

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: Sir! I owe you nothing.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Two hundred and thirteen drachmas, every one to me

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: I am indeed in debt some such amount
To various citizens, but––

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: All to me!
Aha! I have bought up all your debts, and I am now
Your only creditor; and I'll be paid, too!
Pay me, this hour.

sp.speaker: Myr.
sp.l: I cannot.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Then I seize you
Here for my slave–your wife, your daughter, too;
All for my slaves–aha!–Now you may mock
And gibe at Polydor !–You, and this woman
I'll sell for rubbish, but this pretty pert one
I'll keep–
sp.stage: [Ingomar springs on him, and seizes him.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Dog! hound! down to her feet and ask for mercy!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Help–citizens!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Hold, Ingemar! It is too true, it is the law.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Law! to make you his slave!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Alas! such is his right–harm him not, then.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: She bids me spare thee, or I had, ere this,
Crushed thee beneath my heel; –what dost thou want?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Two hundred and thirteen drachmas – I'll not bate one.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: But, man, they have it not.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: They have themselves :
I'll take themselves, –I will not lose my money.

sp.speaker: Act.
sp.l: Parthenia shall wed thee.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: I'll not have her.
Aha! I'll have my money or my slaves–
So, come.

sp.speaker: Ing.
sp.l: Hold–stay! thou art fixed to have this?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.l: Ay,
Either in gold or flesh.

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Will nothing move thee?

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: My money or my slaves.

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Wait––

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: Not one moment.
Come slaves!

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Stay–you are fixed to have the worth
Of your two hundred drachmas?

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: And thirteen !
I'll not abate a piece.

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Well, I promise thee
A slave worth more than all your money.

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: Where?

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Here!

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: Who ?

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Myself.

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: Oh, no–heed him not–he's mad!

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Wert thou mad when thou didst give up thyself
A pledge for what thou lovedst?
Come, hasten, take thy slave !

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: Take thee! a firebrand into my house!

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Beware! lay but a finger
On her or what she loves, and thou shalt know
What 'tis to live with Ingomar, thy foe.
In vain Massilia's legions shall surround thee–
In the market, amidst thy traffic, in thy home,
Thy bed, in the dark midnight, there shall still
Ingomar's eye glare on thee: thou shalt find
Thyself with Ingomar alone!

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: Hold! mercy!
I will consent–I–
Oh, the whip, the chain
Shall make him pay for this!

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Give me those papers,
Now, Myron, thou art free! All, all are free.

sp.speaker: Parta.
sp.l: Oh, misery!

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: And now, old man, although unwillingly,
Thou hast kept thy word, yet will I freely mine.
I will work for thee, truly, diligently,
And weep not–cling not to me thus, Parthenia;–
Of all the joys with which thou hast cheered my soul,
This is the purest, holiest. The slavery
That gives thee freedom, brings along with it
So rich a treasure of consoling joy,
Liberty shall be poor and worthless by its side.

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: I'll put thee to the proof–come, slave! Ah, help!
What do I see? the enemy! the barbarians!
Treachery! the city's taken! Oh, my gold!

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Peace, fool! do you not see they bear green boughs?
They come in peace–they are ambassasors,

div.stage: Enter the Timarch, with Attendants, with him Alastor, Novio, and several of the Allemanni bearing green boughs. R. U. E.

sp.speaker: Timar.
sp.l: Behold the man you seek!

sp.speaker: Alast.
sp.l: Ingomar!
sp.stage: (Ingomar rushes to them and greets them.

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Novio! why come you here?

sp.speaker: Alast.
sp.l: We heard a rumour
One of our people was a prisoner
Within these walls: and paused, upon our way
Against the Allobrogi, to ask its truth.

sp.speaker: Timar.
sp.l: He is free as yourselves.

sp.speaker: Alast.
sp.l: Silence, and let him speak. Ingomar, speak!
If thou, the pride and glory of our race,
Art here under restraint, though but the lightest,
We have a force without shall quickly level
These vile walls with the dust and bear thee off
In triumph from them. Say, art thou free?

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Timar.
sp.l: No?

sp.speaker: Alast.
sp.l: What art thou, then?

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: A slave.

sp.speaker: Alast.
sp.l: Pass round the sword without! – to the attack!–
Down with the walls!

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Hold! and let no man stir.
How! think you Ingomar would live a slave,
But by his own submission.

sp.speaker: Alast.
sp.l: Where's the chief, then,
The mighty warrior who has vanquished thee?
I burn to look on him.

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.stage: (pointing to Polydor, who has crept into R., corner)
sp.l: Behold him there!

sp.speaker: Alast.
sp.l: Ah, he!

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: Help! mercy! help!

sp.speaker: Timar.
sp.stage: (who has been talking with Myron, advances.)
sp.l: Oh! noble, matchless man.
Take back thy liberty–my word confers it.

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Not so–
My honor pledged me yonder creature's slave,
For a condition; he has granted that:
My faith is pledged, and must be kept: who would
That Ingomar were free, must pay his ransom.

sp.speaker: Timar.
sp.l: That be my privilege. (to attendants) Discharge this ransom.
Be justice done–but not imperfectly–
More justice rests behind. When he is paid,
See he collects his wealth, all that he owns;
Then drive him forth beyond the city walls–
Masilia's shame and scorn.

sp.speaker: Poly.
sp.l: Mercy, great Timarch!
The barbarians are without, they'll plunder me!

sp.speaker: Timar.
sp.l: See thou to that. Away with him!
Noble Ingomar,
If such as thou the Alemanni breed
They must be made Massilia's friends, allies,
At any honorable price.
A few hours back we offered thee a house,
Lands, and this maid for wife.

sp.speaker: Alast.
sp.l: The Greek girl! then
He is lost to us. Farewell–peace to Massilia!

sp.speaker: Timar.
sp.l: We must have more than peace–fellowship,friendship,
Let us be brothers–land shall be assigned you
To found a city near us, of which city
We name thee, Ingomar, the Timarch.

sp.speaker: Myron.
sp.l: There, wife! dost hear? our son–in–law a Timarch!
Who is right now? How, Ingomar, not a word?

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Oh, hush! my swelling heart has only room
For one thought, for one word–Parthenia, mine,
For ever mine! (embracing her.) To love I owe this bliss.

sp.speaker: Parth.
sp.l: To love and honour.

sp.speaker: Ingo.
sp.l: Ah! now, indeed, for ever we are joined–
Two souls with but a single thought.
Two hearts that beat as one.'

div.stage: Guards. Allemanni. Citizens.
Actea. Myron. Timarch, Parth. Ingo. Alastor. Ambr. Nov.
R. L.
Curtain.
